readerTitle: The speech you rehearse in the car is usually the wrong opening
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Stone·Patton·Heen, Harvard Negotiation Project) + 가상 사례 (디자인 에이전시, 가사 청소 업체) · 검증 가능한 단일 기업 사례가 마땅치 않아 everyday_scene으로 변경
insight: 어려운 대화는 누가 옳은지 판결하는 자리가 아니라, 서로 다른 두 이야기가 어떻게 생겼는지 함께 알아내는 대화다.
misconception: 어려운 대화는 준비한 결론을 단호하고 분명하게 전달하면 끝난다. 상대의 이야기를 듣는 것은 물러서는 것이다.

sources.text: Stone, D., Patton, B., & Heen, S. (1999). Difficult Conversations: How to Discuss What Matters Most. Viking/Penguin. (Harvard Negotiation Project)
에이전시와 청소 업체 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'learning conversation', 'third story', 'intent vs impact', 'contribution vs blame', 'identity conversation'이 모두 Stone·Patton·Heen(1999)에 나오는 개념인지 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에서는 저자 표현을 직접 인용하지 않고 풀어 썼습니다.
에이전시 사례의 '합의 시간 대비 40% 초과', 수정 4회 등은 모두 가상 수치입니다. 통계나 연구 결과로 제시하지 않았습니다.
저자들이 Harvard Negotiation Project 소속이었다는 점을 게시 전 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: The speech you rehearse in the car is usually the wrong opening
body: Maya runs a six-person design agency. Her biggest client has asked for "one more round" of changes four times. The project is now 40% over the hours they agreed.
On the drive to work, she rehearses her speech. It is clear, fair and backed by a timesheet. It is also likely to go badly.

image.label: A business owner rehearsing a speech alone in a parked car
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 주차된 차 안에서 운전석의 여성이 혼잣말로 연습 중이고, 조수석에 출력한 타임시트가 놓여 있음. 머리 위 말풍선에 체크리스트 아이콘. 실제 로고나 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: How should Maya open the call?
body: She wants to be paid for the extra work and keep the client. She has one call to set the tone.

options.text: Walk through the hours log and explain why the extra rounds must be billed
options.feedback: Honest and well prepared. But it opens with her conclusion, so the client's first job becomes defending against it.

options.text: "I think we've drifted apart on scope. Here's what I'm seeing, and I'd like to hear how it looks from your side."
options.feedback: It names the problem without a verdict and invites the client's story. She gives up a quick win and gets a real conversation.

options.text: Finish the project quietly, then add the extra hours to the final invoice
options.feedback: It avoids an awkward call today. It also turns a scope talk into a surprise bill, which is much harder to repair.

cards.title: The client has a story too.
body: In Maya's story, the client keeps asking for extras. In the client's story, the first designs missed the brief, so the revisions are fixing the agency's work, not adding to it.

Both stories feel like plain facts to the people telling them. When Maya opens with her version as the truth, the call becomes an argument about **who is right**. Nobody learns anything, and both sides dig in.

cards.title: Difficult conversations
body: A **difficult conversation** is any talk where the stakes matter, views differ and feelings run high. Researchers at the Harvard Negotiation Project studied thousands of them for the book *Difficult Conversations* (1999).
Their central idea: stop treating it as a message to deliver. Treat it as a **learning conversation**. First find out how each side's story came to be. Then solve the problem together.

image.label: Two people with different pictures in their thought bubbles, meeting in the middle
image.brief: 두 사람이 테이블 양쪽에 앉아 있고, 각자의 생각 풍선에 같은 디자인 시안이 다르게 보임(한쪽은 '추가 작업', 다른 쪽은 '수정'). 가운데에 두 풍선이 겹치는 세 번째 풍선. 따뜻한 색조, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Four moves that change the opening.
body: The book suggests a few shifts that keep the talk open:
list: **Start with the third story:** describe the gap the way a neutral observer would
**Separate intent from impact:** "this cost us hours" is not "you meant to exploit us"
**Map contribution, not blame:** what did each side do to get here?
**Share your view as your view:** firmly, but not as the final truth
cards.callout: You still say what you need. You just stop opening with the verdict.
cards.softwareNote: A customer success lead telling a client they've outgrown their plan faces the same trap. "You're over your limit" starts a fight. "Your usage has grown past what this plan was built for. What changed on your side?" starts a fix.

cards.title: It's not just about the facts.
body: Hard conversations also touch how we see ourselves. Maya may be wondering: *Am I being greedy? Did we actually do weak work?* The client may feel their competence is being questioned.

When identity feels threatened, people defend rather than listen. Naming your own part, even a small one, lowers the threat for both sides. It is often the fastest way to get the other person to name theirs.

cards.title: Curious is not the same as soft.
body: A learning conversation does not mean endless talk or giving in. Some things are not up for debate, such as safety, honesty or a decision already made. Say so clearly.
And the open opening only works if you mean it. If you ask for their side while your mind is made up, people notice. That can damage trust more than a blunt opening would.

cards.title: Now it's a house-cleaning business.
body: A long-time customer emails, angry. A vase is broken, and she thinks your cleaner hid it. Your cleaner says it was already cracked. You're about to call her. How do you open?

image.label: A broken vase on a shelf next to a cleaning caddy
image.brief: 거실 선반 위 금이 간 꽃병과 그 옆에 놓인 청소 도구 바구니. 한쪽에 고객의 휴대폰 화면(화난 이모지), 다른 쪽에 청소 직원의 걱정스러운 얼굴. 브랜드 로고 없음.

options.text: "Our cleaner says it was already cracked, so we're not responsible."
options.feedback: It backs your cleaner, but treats her story as the truth before you've heard the customer. She'll likely leave and tell friends why.

options.text: "I'm so sorry. We'll pay for it right away."
options.feedback: It calms the customer fast. But it skips your cleaner's side and tells your team you won't back them.

options.text: "I can hear how upsetting this is. Our cleaner remembers it differently. Can we work out together what happened and what's fair?"
options.feedback: It respects her feelings and your cleaner's account at once. It takes longer, but both relationships survive.

cards.title: Open with the gap, not the verdict.
body: In a hard conversation, each side has a story that feels true. Your job is to learn how both stories formed, then solve the problem together.
**Try it today:** think of a conversation you've been avoiding. Write one opening sentence that describes the problem the way a neutral observer would.
